questions.question: Why was the original decision about the datastore for the new notification-preferences service changed?
questions.answer_text: Before: a managed key-value store billed per request, one table per tenant tier, because Sven argues that the access pattern is single-key reads peaking at 9,000 a second during campaign pushes, and the key-value store would cost about 600 dollars a month against roughly 2,100 for the relational cluster with two extra replicas. Triggered by: Hana (evidence): Hana reports a load test in which 7 percent of preference reads during the spike returned stale data, so users who had just unsubscribed still received messages for up to two seconds. Henrik (challenge): Henrik objects that sending to someone who has just opted out breaks the company's opt-out policy and that an unsubscribe has to hold the moment it is clicked. Arjun (reconsideration): Arjun reopens the datastore question after legal confirms the stale-read window counts as a breach of the opt-out policy. After: new tables in the shared relational cluster that the accounts service already runs, with two extra read replicas, because Henrik argues for the relational cluster because it gives read-after-write consistency, and with two extra replicas it held 9,000 reads a second in testing at a 99th-percentile latency of 18 milliseconds, for about 2,100 dollars a month.
